narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 77.4% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because the law school sets a high bar for admission and this probability is well above their threshold, your application was rejected.

The three factors that mattered most to this decision were your academic performance in law school, your LSAT score, and your first-year grades. Your third-year class ranking had the strongest influence and pushed the prediction strongly toward failure. Standing in only the second decile—far below the average of roughly the sixth decile among accepted students—signaled that you struggled to keep pace with your peers later in the program. Your first-year ranking in the second decile similarly worked against you, reinforcing the impression of consistent academic difficulty.

Your LSAT score of 43 worked in the opposite direction. It is noticeably higher than the average of 37 among accepted students and therefore pulled the prediction toward passing. However, this positive effect was not large enough to overcome the two strong signals coming from your class rankings.

Given these results, you should focus on strengthening the areas that hurt your profile the most. Consider retaking key courses to improve your academic record, or explore bar-preparation programs that have helped students with similar grade trajectories succeed on the exam. With targeted improvement you can raise your chances on a future application or on the bar itself. (248 words)
